narrative:
Sunday has morning sun, scattered afternoon clouds, and isolated afternoon showers and thunderstorms. Temperatures are warmer than Saturday but only a few degrees above the late-August average. The story of the week becomes heat--temperatures climb progressively warmer through Wednesday and hold into Thursday. Wednesday and Thursday approach records for the dates. Isolated afternoon showers and thunderstorms may become welcome heat relief for some.

Subscribe Forecast Discussion A large ridge of high pressure builds over the Southeast early this week, and it runs the show. Under a ridge, air generally sinks, limiting afternoon showers and thunderstorms; skies stay mostly sunny, and heat builds day by day. Sunday sits on the ridge's front edge. Leftover weekend moisture supports isolated afternoon showers and thunderstorms. Most locations stay dry. Monday and Tuesday belong to the ridge. Sunshine dominates, and each day runs warmer than the last. I cannot rule out an isolated afternoon mountain storm. Wednesday and Thursday are the peak of the heat, with temperatures approaching records for the dates. By Thursday the ridge erodes on its northern edge. Thunderstorms increase in coverage Thursday afternoon, lingering into early evening. Friday is almost as warm, with isolated or widely scattered afternoon and evening shower/thunderstorm coverage. A cold front comes to the rescue Saturday night. We may see a period of enhanced showers and thunderstorms Saturday, but timing remains in doubt from this far out. Relief from the heat arrives early next week. Detailed forecast discussion and analysis is only available to RaysWeather supporters. All Photos Submit Photo Latest Insights September 2026 Forecast Outlook Forecast Monthly Forecast September 2026 Weather Outlook Southern Appalachians – SW Virginia & Western North Carolina September 2026 will open very warm, then trend gradually toward typical September weather as the month goes on. After two wet months, the pattern turns drier than average — with a tropical season held down by El Niño as the one wildcard. The lead graphic for this document shows expected overall monthly anomalies for both temperature (warmer) and precipitation (drier). The Typical September: Summertime Slipping Away Well, the sun's not so hot in the sky today
And you know I can see summertime slipping on away
A few more geese are gone, a few more leaves turning red
But the grass is as soft as a feather in a featherbed
— James Taylor, "September Grass" James Taylor has it right. September is the month the mountains change their mind about summer. August gives up almost nothing; September gives up a lot, and most of it in the second half. The average high falls nine to ten degrees between the first of the month and the last, and the nights lead the way, cooling faster than the days. The rain changes character more than amount. September is nearly as wet as August on average, but the afternoon thunderstorms that ruled the summer fade. The Foothills dry out more than the mountains — North Wilkesboro and Hickory average half an inch to an inch less rainfall than in August. The high peaks are different: Mt Mitchell, on average, is wetter in September than August. And this is the peak of hurricane season, when a single tropical remnant has produced some of the region's largest rain totals. A September tropical event in the area decides how the month is remembered. The Big Picture for September 2026 The month begins with the pattern August never delivered. A large ridge of high pressure aloft builds over the Southeast in the first days of September and holds through the first week. This will be the warmest stretch of the month. The ridge then slides slowly west, over Tennessee and Kentucky and on toward the southern Mississippi Valley. Behind it, a weak trough settles into the eastern United States and briefly turns our flow more northwesterly. A front accompanies that change September 8 to 10. We will have noticeably cooler weather after that front. The eastern trough erodes later in week two. The rest of the month features a more neutral westerly flow: no strong ridge, no deep trough, no cold intrusions. Temperatures step down gradually toward typical September weather. With the normal temperatures themselves falling nine to ten degrees over the month, September 2026 will feel like a bigger transition month than usual. Precipitation makes the sharper break. July and August both ran wet; September looks drier than average. Tropical activity is the wildcard — September is the heart of a hurricane season inhibited overall by El Niño. Impact from a tropical system here is not expected, but it is not impossible. September Outlook at a Glance |Week|Temperature|Precipitation| |-|-|-| |Week 1 (September 1–7)|Well above average|Below average| |Week 2 (September 8–14)|Near average|Slightly below average| |Week 3 (September 15–21)|Slightly above average|Slightly below average| |Week 4 (September 22–30)|Near average|Slightly below average| |Overall for September|Above average|Slightly below average| Other Items of Note Here are the data sources influencing our September forecast: Three long-range models (from the ECMWF, CMC, and GFS). During the three days in which this forecast was developed, the models went from widely divergent individual predictions for September to good agreement on this warm/dry scenario. We chose the ECMWF for the forecast graphic since it looked the most reasonable across the Southeast. Teleconnections, or large-scale links in atmospheric pressure and climate anomalies: North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO), Arctic Oscillation (AO), Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO), Pacific-North American pattern (PNA). All of these tend to have weak correlations to our weather this time of year, but all were particularly weak signals and unhelpful this year. The currently strong and strengthening El Niño also has weak correlations to our weather this time of year (except to weaken tropical system development). But because it is about to become a major player in our weather, it will get its own section for discussion below. As always, this forecast is built from scratch. We work from the data to reach our own conclusions, then check the NOAA Climate Prediction Center outlook for comparison. This month our conclusions are close to the NOAA September Outlook. Climatological Averages for September |Location|Avg High (°F)|Avg Low (°F)|Avg Precip (in)| |-|-|-|-| |Asheville|78.7|58.0|3.67| |Asheville Airport|78.7|57.9|4.13| |Banner Elk|71.3|51.5|4.55| |Beech Mountain|63.4|50.5|4.99| |Boone|72.2|50.3|5.73| |Burnsville|75.9|53.9|4.21| |Galax|74.8|53.0|4.46| |Hendersonville|77.5|56.4|4.97| |Hickory|79.8|60.9|3.93| |Jefferson|75.2|50.3|4.35| |Lenoir|80.4|58.9|4.25| |Marion|79.1|59.9|4.75| |Marshall|79.4|53.5|3.36| |Morganton|80.0|58.5|4.59| |Mt Mitchell|61.4|46.2|8.76| |North Wilkesboro|79.4|58.0|4.25| |Sparta|75.0|52.7|5.13| |Waynesville|75.6|52.9|4.25| |Wytheville|76.5|52.8|3.36| The Ocean: El Niño Reaches for the Record Book A historic El Niño is strengthening on schedule. The warmest water still hugs the coast of South America. The warmth tapers westward toward the central Pacific. That east-loaded shape is the classic form of El Niño. That classic shape matters for winter: events with heat concentrated in the eastern Pacific produce the most reliable response over North America, strengthening the subtropical jet and steering storms along the Gulf Coast and up the East Coast — creating opportunities for strong winter storms in the Southern Appalachians. The graphic below shows Sea Surface Temperature anomalies across the globe; note the equatorial Pacific—that’s a strong El Niño in progress. Last month we said this would be a very strong El Niño. It will be — and it has the potential to become the strongest on record. The event peaks in late fall, holds through early winter before gradually fading in late winter and spring. (See the graphic below showing model guidance for when El Niño will peak.) The strongest El Niños since 1950 (when detailed records began) were in 1982-83, 1997-98, and 2015-16. Forecasts at this point in their development tend to overshoot peaks, so we say potential rather than certainty for the record. “Very strong” is not in doubt. For the season ahead, the outline has not changed. Strong, east-based El Niño winters in the Southern Appalachians run wetter than normal, with an active southern storm track delivering more systems than an average year. The winter looks to have stronger and more frequent storms; some of these may produce significant snow in the mountains. However, the same system that gives Beech, Sugar, and Bald Mountains and Mt Mitchell over a foot can give the Foothills just a cold rain. That does not mean the Foothills escape snow and ice; it means precipitation type will be the hard call. We will have much more to say in the RaysWeather.com Fearless Forecast for Winter 2026-27, published the third week of October. Although not directly related to the El Niño, another ocean anomaly is fading in the Atlantic with potential impact on our weather. The cool patch in the Gulf of Guinea (off the coast of West Africa) is called an Atlantic Niña. It has faded to something barely detectable, so El Niño's wind shear now stands alone as the main brake on the Atlantic hurricane season. The rest of the world's oceans remain unusually warm — the background that gives us warmer nights and heavier downpours when rain does come. Aug 30, 2026 WWR?- Doc Watson Where in the Weather is Ray?
